Collections - List, Set and Map.explanation: Java Collections Framework provides interfaces and classes for storing and manipulating groups of objects. List maintains an ordered collection and allows duplicates, Set stores unique elements, and Map stores key-value pairs. Common implementations include ArrayList, LinkedList, HashSet, LinkedHashSet, TreeSet, HashMap, LinkedHashMap, and TreeMap.

List Introduction.explanation: List is an ordered collection that allows duplicate elements. Elements can be accessed using their index. Common List implementations are ArrayList and LinkedList.
List Introduction.example: A List can store student names where duplicate names are allowed.
points_to_remember: List maintains insertion order.
List allows duplicate elements.
List supports index-based access.
Common implementations include ArrayList and LinkedList.

ArrayList.explanation: ArrayList is a resizable-array implementation of the List interface. It provides fast random access using indexes.
ArrayList.example: ArrayList is useful when frequent reading by index is required.
points_to_remember: ArrayList is dynamically resizable.
It maintains insertion order.
It allows duplicates and null values.
Random access using get() is efficient.
Insertion or removal in the middle can require shifting elements.

LinkedList.explanation: LinkedList is a doubly linked implementation of List and Deque. It supports operations at both ends and can be useful when frequent insertions or removals occur at known positions.
LinkedList.example: LinkedList can be used as both a List and a queue/deque.
points_to_remember: LinkedList implements List and Deque.
It maintains insertion order.
It allows duplicates and null values.
It provides addFirst() and addLast().
Random index-based access is slower than ArrayList.

List add().explanation: add() inserts an element into a List. It can add an element at the end or at a specified index.
List add().example: An element can be added either at the end or at a specific index.
points_to_remember: add(element) adds at the end.
add(index, element) inserts at a specific position.
Adding at an index shifts later elements.

List get().explanation: get() retrieves an element from a List using its index.
points_to_remember: Indexes start from 0.
An invalid index causes IndexOutOfBoundsException.
ArrayList provides efficient index-based access.

List set().explanation: set() replaces the element at a specified index.
points_to_remember: set() replaces an existing element.
It does not increase the List size.
The specified index must already exist.

List remove().explanation: remove() removes an element either by index or by object.
List remove().example: An element can be removed using its value or index.
points_to_remember: remove(index) removes by position.
remove(object) removes the first matching object.
Removing an element changes the List size.

List contains().explanation: contains() checks whether a List contains a specified element.
List contains().example: The result is true because Java exists in the List.
points_to_remember: contains() returns boolean.
It uses equals() semantics to determine matching elements.

List indexOf() and lastIndexOf().explanation: indexOf() returns the first occurrence of an element, while lastIndexOf() returns the last occurrence.
List indexOf() and lastIndexOf().example: The first Java occurs at index 0 and the last Java occurs at index 2.
points_to_remember: indexOf() searches from the beginning.
lastIndexOf() searches from the end.
Both return -1 when no match exists.

List size() and isEmpty().explanation: size() returns the number of elements in a collection, while isEmpty() checks whether the collection contains no elements.
List size() and isEmpty().example: An empty List has size 0 and isEmpty() returns true.
points_to_remember: size() returns the number of elements.
isEmpty() returns true when size is zero.

List clear().explanation: clear() removes all elements from a List.
List clear().example: After clear(), the List becomes empty.
points_to_remember: clear() removes all elements.
The List object itself remains usable.
After clearing, size() returns 0.

List removeIf().explanation: removeIf() removes all elements that satisfy a specified predicate.
points_to_remember: removeIf() accepts a Predicate.
Every matching element is removed.
It modifies the collection.

List sort().explanation: sort() sorts a List according to its natural ordering or a supplied Comparator.
points_to_remember: sort(null) uses natural ordering.
A Comparator can define custom ordering.
sort() modifies the List.

Set Introduction.explanation: Set is a Collection that does not allow duplicate elements. Common implementations include HashSet, LinkedHashSet, and TreeSet.
Set Introduction.example: Adding Java twice still stores only one Java element.
points_to_remember: Set does not allow duplicate elements.
Set does not provide index-based access.
HashSet is commonly used for fast membership checks.
Set ordering depends on its implementation.

HashSet.explanation: HashSet is a Set implementation based on hashing. It provides efficient basic operations such as add, remove, and contains on average.
HashSet.example: The duplicate value 10 is stored only once.
points_to_remember: HashSet does not allow duplicates.
HashSet does not guarantee iteration order.
It permits one null element.
It is based on hashing.

LinkedHashSet.explanation: LinkedHashSet is a HashSet variant that maintains insertion order during iteration.
LinkedHashSet.example: Elements are iterated in the order in which they were inserted.
points_to_remember: Duplicates are not allowed.
Insertion order is maintained.
It generally uses more memory than HashSet because of linked structure.

TreeSet.explanation: TreeSet is a NavigableSet implementation that keeps elements sorted according to their natural ordering or a supplied Comparator.
TreeSet.example: The values are stored in sorted order: [10, 20, 30].
points_to_remember: TreeSet maintains sorted order.
Duplicates are not allowed.
TreeSet provides navigation methods such as first(), last(), lower(), and higher().
Elements must be mutually comparable or a suitable Comparator must be supplied.

Set add().explanation: add() inserts an element into a Set. If the element already exists, the Set remains unchanged.
Set add().example: The first add returns true, while the second returns false because Java already exists.
points_to_remember: add() returns true when the Set changes.
It returns false when the element already exists.
Sets automatically prevent duplicates.

Set contains().explanation: contains() checks whether a Set contains a specified element.
Set contains().example: The result is true because Java is present.
points_to_remember: contains() returns boolean.
HashSet provides efficient average-case membership checks.

Set remove().explanation: remove() removes a specified element from a Set if it exists.
Set remove().example: Java is removed from the Set.
points_to_remember: remove() returns true when an element is removed.
It returns false when the element does not exist.

Set Union.explanation: Union combines all unique elements from two sets. It can be implemented using addAll().
points_to_remember: addAll() combines elements.
Duplicates are automatically removed by the Set.
The original sets can remain unchanged when working on a copy.

Set Intersection.explanation: Intersection contains only elements that are present in both sets. It can be implemented using retainAll().
points_to_remember: retainAll() keeps only common elements.
retainAll() modifies the collection on which it is called.

Set Difference.explanation: Difference contains elements that exist in one set but not in another. It can be implemented using removeAll().
points_to_remember: removeAll() removes elements found in another collection.
The operation modifies the original Set.

Map Introduction.explanation: Map stores data as key-value pairs. Each key can occur only once, while multiple keys can have the same value.
Map Introduction.example: A student ID can be used as a key and the student's name as the value.
points_to_remember: Map stores key-value pairs.
Keys are unique.
Values can be duplicated.
Map is not a subtype of Collection.

HashMap.explanation: HashMap is a hash-table-based Map implementation that provides efficient average-case lookup, insertion, and removal.
HashMap.example: A HashMap can associate student names with their scores.
points_to_remember: Keys are unique.
HashMap does not guarantee iteration order.
HashMap permits one null key and multiple null values.
It provides efficient average-case basic operations.

LinkedHashMap.explanation: LinkedHashMap is a HashMap variant that maintains a predictable iteration order, normally insertion order.
LinkedHashMap.example: Entries are iterated in insertion order.
points_to_remember: Keys are unique.
Insertion order is maintained by default.
It can also be configured for access-order iteration.
It permits one null key and multiple null values.

TreeMap.explanation: TreeMap is a NavigableMap implementation that stores entries sorted according to key ordering.
TreeMap.example: The keys are maintained in sorted order: 10, 20, 30.
points_to_remember: Keys are sorted.
Keys must be mutually comparable or a Comparator must be provided.
TreeMap provides navigation methods.
TreeMap does not permit null keys under natural ordering.

Map put().explanation: put() inserts or updates a key-value mapping in a Map.
Map put().example: The second put for key 1 replaces Java with C++.
points_to_remember: Keys must be unique.
Putting an existing key replaces its value.
put() returns the previous value associated with the key, or null if there was no mapping.

Map get().explanation: get() retrieves the value associated with a specified key.
points_to_remember: get() returns the associated value.
If the key does not exist, get() returns null.
Use getOrDefault() when a fallback value is useful.

Map getOrDefault().explanation: getOrDefault() returns the value associated with a key or a specified default value when the key is absent.
Map getOrDefault().example: Because Python is absent, the result is 0.
points_to_remember: It avoids explicit null checking for simple fallback behavior.
The Map is not modified by getOrDefault().

Map containsKey().explanation: containsKey() checks whether a specified key exists in a Map.
Map containsKey().example: The result is true because key 101 exists.
points_to_remember: containsKey() returns boolean.
It is useful before retrieving or updating a mapping.

Map containsValue().explanation: containsValue() checks whether at least one mapping contains a specified value.
Map containsValue().example: The result is true because Alice exists as a value.
points_to_remember: containsValue() returns boolean.
Unlike keys, values do not need to be unique.

Map remove().explanation: remove() removes a mapping associated with a specified key. An overload can also remove only when a key-value pair matches.
Map remove().example: The mapping with key 1 is removed.
points_to_remember: remove(key) removes the mapping for the key.
remove(key, value) removes only when both match.
remove() returns the previous value or null when appropriate.

Map replace().explanation: replace() updates the value associated with an existing key.
Map replace().example: The value Java is replaced with Python.
points_to_remember: replace() changes an existing mapping.
It does not add a new key when the key is absent.
replace(key, oldValue, newValue) performs conditional replacement.

Map putIfAbsent().explanation: putIfAbsent() inserts a mapping only when the specified key does not already have a mapping.
Map putIfAbsent().example: Java remains associated with 90 while Python is added with 80.
points_to_remember: Existing mappings are not overwritten.
Useful for initializing values only when absent.

Map computeIfAbsent().explanation: computeIfAbsent() computes and associates a value when a key is not already associated with a non-null value.
Map computeIfAbsent().example: The value 4 is calculated and associated with Java.
points_to_remember: The mapping function is used when the key is absent or mapped to null.
Useful for lazy value creation.
The mapping function should return null only when no mapping should be recorded.

Map computeIfPresent().explanation: computeIfPresent() recalculates a value when a key already has a non-null mapping.
points_to_remember: The mapping function receives the key and current value.
If the function returns null, the mapping is removed.

Map compute().explanation: compute() recalculates the value associated with a key whether or not a previous mapping exists.
Map compute().example: The value associated with Java becomes 11.
points_to_remember: compute() can create or update a mapping.
The mapping function receives the key and current value.
Returning null removes the mapping.

Map merge().explanation: merge() combines a new value with an existing value using a specified remapping function.
Map merge().example: The value for Java becomes 3 after merging 1 and 2.
points_to_remember: If the key is absent, the supplied value is inserted.
If the key exists, the remapping function combines the values.
Returning null from the remapping function removes the mapping.

Map keySet().explanation: keySet() returns a Set view containing all keys in the Map.
Map keySet().example: The result contains the keys 1 and 2.
points_to_remember: keySet() returns a view, not an independent copy.
Changes to the Map can be reflected in the returned Set.
Useful for iterating over keys.

Map values().explanation: values() returns a Collection view containing all values in the Map.
Map values().example: The result contains the values Java and Python.
points_to_remember: values() returns a view.
Values can contain duplicates.
Useful when only values need to be processed.

Map entrySet().explanation: entrySet() returns a Set view of Map.Entry objects representing key-value pairs.
Map entrySet().example: entrySet() is commonly used when both keys and values are required during iteration.
points_to_remember: entrySet() returns Map.Entry objects.
getKey() retrieves the key.
getValue() retrieves the value.
It is commonly used for efficient Map iteration.

Map forEach().explanation: forEach() performs an action for each key-value mapping.
Map forEach().example: Each key-value pair is processed using a lambda expression.
points_to_remember: forEach() accepts a BiConsumer.
It provides both the key and value.
The iteration order depends on the Map implementation.

Map replaceAll().explanation: replaceAll() replaces every Map value using a remapping function.
points_to_remember: replaceAll() processes every mapping.
The remapping function receives the key and value.
It modifies the Map.

Map size() and isEmpty().explanation: size() returns the number of mappings in a Map, while isEmpty() checks whether the Map contains no mappings.
Map size() and isEmpty().example: An empty Map has size 0 and isEmpty() returns true.
points_to_remember: size() counts key-value mappings.
isEmpty() returns true when there are no mappings.

Map clear().explanation: clear() removes all key-value mappings from a Map.
Map clear().example: The Map becomes empty after clear().
points_to_remember: clear() removes every mapping.
The Map object remains usable afterward.

Map replaceAll and compute operations.explanation: Modern Map APIs provide functional methods such as compute, computeIfAbsent, computeIfPresent, merge, and replaceAll for concise value manipulation.
Map replaceAll and compute operations.example: These methods allow values to be initialized, updated, merged, and transformed using lambda expressions.
points_to_remember: computeIfAbsent() initializes missing values.
computeIfPresent() updates existing values.
compute() can handle both absent and present keys.
merge() combines values.
replaceAll() transforms every mapping.

Collections Utility Class.explanation: java.util.Collections provides static utility methods for working with Collection objects such as Lists, including sorting, reversing, shuffling, searching, and finding minimum or maximum elements.
Collections Utility Class.example: Collections.sort() sorts a List and Collections.reverse() reverses its order.
points_to_remember: Collections is a utility class.
sort() sorts a List.
reverse() reverses a List.
shuffle() randomly reorders a List.
min() and max() find minimum and maximum elements.
binarySearch() searches a sorted List.

Collection Iteration.explanation: Java collections can be traversed using enhanced for loops, iterators, streams, and forEach().
Collection Iteration.example: Iterator allows sequential traversal through a collection.
points_to_remember: Iterator provides hasNext() and next().
Iterator can safely remove elements using remove().
Enhanced for loops provide simpler iteration.
Streams provide functional-style processing.

Iterator.explanation: Iterator is an interface used to traverse elements of a Collection sequentially.
Iterator.example: Iterator can remove the current element safely during iteration.
points_to_remember: hasNext() checks whether another element exists.
next() returns the next element.
remove() removes the last element returned by next().
Direct structural modification during iteration can cause ConcurrentModificationException.

ListIterator.explanation: ListIterator is an Iterator specifically for Lists and supports bidirectional traversal as well as element insertion and replacement.
ListIterator.example: ListIterator can move both forward and backward through a List.
points_to_remember: ListIterator supports forward and backward traversal.
hasNext() checks forward elements.
hasPrevious() checks backward elements.
It provides add(), set(), and remove().
It is available only for Lists.

List.ArrayList: Resizable array, fast random access, preserves insertion order, allows duplicates.
List.LinkedList: Doubly linked list, supports List and Deque operations, preserves insertion order, allows duplicates.

Set.HashSet: Unique elements, no guaranteed iteration order, hashing-based.

Map.HashMap: Key-value storage, no guaranteed iteration order, hashing-based.
Map.LinkedHashMap: Key-value storage with predictable insertion-order iteration by default.

summary: List stores ordered elements and allows duplicates.
ArrayList is commonly used for fast index-based access.
LinkedList supports both List and Deque operations.
HashSet provides hash-based storage without guaranteed iteration order.
TreeMap maintains keys in sorted order.
List provides index-based operations such as get() and set().
Set provides set operations such as addAll(), retainAll(), and removeAll().
Map provides key-value operations such as put(), get(), remove(), and compute().
entrySet(), keySet(), and values() provide different views of a Map.
Iterator and ListIterator provide controlled collection traversal.
The Collections utility class provides additional algorithms for working with collections.
